title: Yom Kippur: Jonah
hook: the afternoon reads Jonah, and the whole city of Nineveh turns

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Avodah, the high priest's day. Your line was once a year. What's your once-a-year thing? Today, the late afternoon of Yom Kippur, when people are hungry and tired, and someone reads a story about a fish. Day six hundred fifty-six.

It's three or four in the afternoon. The fast is nearly a day old. Heads ache. Somebody's dozing in the back row. And now, at the afternoon service, the reader chants the whole book of Jonah. Four short chapters. A prophet runs away from God, gets thrown off a ship in a storm, spends three days inside a great fish, and finally goes where he was sent. The fish is what sticks. But the reason to read it today comes after the fish.
screen: `THREE IN THE AFTERNOON, FASTING.` → `A PROPHET RUNS.` → `AFTER THE FISH.`

segments.voice: Jonah is sent to Nineveh, that great city, the capital of Israel's enemy. He runs. Later he says why: he knew God was gracious and would relent, and he didn't want the city spared. When he finally arrives, his whole sermon is five Hebrew words: yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown. And then, astonishingly, it works. The people of Nineveh believe. They fast. Everyone puts on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. The king gets up from his throne, sits in ashes, and orders even the animals to fast. And then the line: "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, which He said He would do unto them; and He did it not." The Mishnah, in tractate Taanit, points out exactly what that verse says and doesn't say. It doesn't say God saw their sackcloth and their fasting. It says God saw their works. Their deeds changed. That's a sharp message for a room full of people who are fasting right now. The fast alone, the Mishnah suggests, isn't what's seen. What changes afterward is. The book ends with Jonah angry, sitting outside the city, and God asking him a question about mercy: should I not have pity on Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who can't tell their right hand from their left, "and also much cattle?" The book ends on that question. It doesn't tell us Jonah's answer. If even Nineveh can turn, the reasoning goes, so can anyone in this room.
screen: `NINEVEH, THE ENEMY CITY.` · `FIVE WORDS, AND THEY TURN.` · `NOT THE SACKCLOTH: THEIR WORKS.` · `A BOOK THAT ENDS ON A QUESTION.` · then, large: `EVEN NINEVEH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: believe someone can change. Think of a person you've written off. Not someone dangerous: someone you've decided is just like that and always will be. A relative, an old friend, a coworker. Hold their face in your mind. Now imagine them, a year from now, having changed one thing. Let yourself picture it. If you pray, you can pray for their turning, and for your own patience. If not, simply leave the door open a crack. The bell holds the time.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement, whose afternoon reading is Jonah, and a whole enemy city that turned.
Your line: even Nineveh. Today, notice one small change in someone you'd given up on, and tell them you noticed. Day six hundred fifty-six.

screen: `DAY 656 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOM KIPPUR: ONE LONG BLAST.`

howItsDone: At the afternoon (Mincha) service of Yom Kippur, the entire book of Jonah is chanted as the haftarah, followed by verses from Micah in many communities.

pairs: sat in ashes, made even animals fast

myth: the verse says God saw Nineveh's sackcloth and fasting
it says God saw their works: their deeds changed.
the book of Jonah ends with a question
God asks whether He should not pity Nineveh.
Jonah ran away because he feared the people of Nineveh would hurt him
the story suggests he didn't want the enemy city to be given a chance to turn.

fork.setup: you're the king of Nineveh. a foreign prophet says your city will be overthrown in forty days. what do you do?
options: rise from the throne, sit in ashes, and call the whole city to turn.
ignore it; prophets are always wrong.
fork.reveal: the king leads the city in turning, and God sees their works and spares them.

original.note: Hebrew: Nineveh, the capital of Assyria.

trapdoor: what you thought: a children's story about a whale.
what it means: even the enemy city can turn, and what counts is what you do, not the sackcloth.
what a scholar hears: Megillah 31a sets Jonah for Yom Kippur afternoon; Mishnah Taanit 2:1 reads Jonah 3:10 as 'their works.'

sources.quoted: And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, which He said He would do unto them; and He did it not.

notes: Jonah 3:10 and 4:11 (JPS 1917) quoted from memory; verify.
Jonah 3:4 'yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown' is five words in Hebrew (od arba'im yom v'Nineveh nehpachet); confirm.
Jonah's motive for fleeing is inferred from 4:2; the myth reveal says 'the story suggests'.
Mishnah Taanit 2:1 on 'their works, not their sackcloth'; Megillah 31a assigns Jonah to Yom Kippur Mincha; confirm.

Editor review (y2 651-668 pass): Jonah's motive now follows Jonah 4:2 (he knew God would relent) instead of an outside claim that Assyria 'terrorized his people'; cut 'may be the shortest sermon in the Bible' and 'most people remember the fish'; the rabbis' reason for choosing the reading is no longer asserted; 'the fast is not the point' now rests on the Mishnah's emphasis.
